doc.title: Ken Poston interviewed by Monk Rowe, via Zoom, June 4, 2024

chapter: Radio, the Jazz Institute and Kenton
title: Finding scores in garages and founding a West Coast archive
summary: Documentary radio work led him into musicians' garages and attics, and to the idea of a West Coast repository funded by events.

story.theme_name: Radio and television work: staff jobs, shows and broadcasts
story.community_name: Managers, bookers and the business of getting work

blocks.x: important. But as you know, that’s not always the case. And a lot of times — and I think the idea behind the whole thing started back in the KLON days when I started to put — not only was I doing the events but also the radio shows that I’ve always done have been more like kind of documentary oriented. And it seems like doing it on a weekly basis that that would be, you know that I’ve, you know, always put a lot of effort into it, a lot of research and I’m kind of built that way in that I always kind of have to have something that I’m working on. And I’ve always done that. So at night at home I’m reading, doing research, whatever the case may be, but I always kind of need that, whatever we’re working on to really delve into and really go into it deeply. So the radio things become kind of natural from that in putting these documentary type programs together. I’ll go interview the artists, find the music that was needed and so on and so forth. But what I discovered when I was doing these radio shows, and the events as well, is Shorty and all the different guys like Rugolo and all, they had all those things they’d done through the years, but they were in garages, attics, buried underneath things. And I realized there needed to be somewhere that gathered the stuff because what I would end up doing, like when we would do a concert that had something to do with Rugolo, I would be in his garage for two or three days finding all these original scores and then I would see all of Rugolo’s original hand-written scores and acetates of unknown concerts and sessions. And I started to get really excited about all of that because it really augmented the things that we were doing and it enabled us to be able to do the events and present all these things and this was, ‘cause at the time we’re talking about ejazzlines did not exist. I mean there wasn't somewhere that if you wanted to do a concert of, you know, Ernie Wilkins’ music, there was not a place you could go and rent those or buy those. I mean you had to get a hold of Ernie Wilkins and hope that he still had them. And that was the case for all of the things on the West Coast. I mean all those things. You had to find them. And so I did. You know I was able to uncover these things, and then it just naturally led to the idea that well there needs to be a repository on the West Coast for these musicians to leave their materials, and I just kind of decided that that would be something that I would like to do. So it crossed over with the last year or two when I was at KLON and then I dove into that full time for the next several years. And it was a good process because I was able to really work on finding all these things, gathering the materials, making arrangements with the musicians to archive the things, and digitize things, and really, really work on it like on a full time basis and then utilize the events — we would do two big events a year and then smaller ones in between, and those events would subsidize the whole thing. So up until we really started to lose a lot of the original musicians if you will — I say “original” meaning people that were doing the music of, or at least people related to who we’re doing the music of.
